record.paper_title: Trimer Covers in the Triangular Grid: Twenty Mostly Open Problems
record.context_brief: unique all-tiles tiling when a+b=1 mod 3
record.original_question: Let T113(a,b) count tilings of the (a,b)-benzel when both stone orientations are allowed and all three bone orientations are allowed. Whenever a+b is congruent to 1 modulo 3, is it true that T113(a,b) = 1, so that the region has exactly one tiling?

evidence.quote: For 0 <= i, j <= 1 and 0 <= k <= 3 we define Tijk (a, b) as the number of ways to tile the (a, b)-benzel if the set of allowed prototiles contains the right stone iff i = 1, contains the left stone iff j = 1, and contains k of the bones. We say that such a tiling is an i, j, k tiling.

Problem 14: Is it true that T113 = 1 when a+b is 1 (mod 3)? (Note that a + b equiv 1 is the situation in which the Conway-Lagarias invariant coincides with the area of the region being tiled, so that all the tiles must be right-pointing stones.)
Comment: This problem is resolved in the affirmative by Theorem 1.1 of [3].

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the triangular lattice in the plane, partitioned into upward- and downward-pointing unit triangular cells. A "right stone" is a trimer formed by three pairwise-adjacent cells whose configuration is a unit upward-pointing triangle of three cells (one up-cell flanked appropriately to form a small triangle pointing right in the standard convention); a "left stone" is the mirror-image trimer. A "bone" is a trimer formed by three contiguous cells whose centers are collinear; up to orientation there are three bones (vertical, rising, and falling).

For positive integers a, b, the (a,b)-benzel is the region in the triangular grid obtained as follows: take a large hexagonal/triangular region and remove three corner pieces parametrized by a and b in the standard way, producing a region with three-fold pseudo-symmetry whose cells can be covered by trimers (stones and bones).

Let T_{1,1,3}(a,b) denote the number of trimer covers (tilings) of the (a,b)-benzel using prototiles drawn from the set { right stone, left stone, vertical bone, rising bone, falling bone } — i.e. both stone orientations and all three bone orientations are permitted.

Prove or disprove: whenever a + b ≡ 1 (mod 3), one has
   T_{1,1,3}(a,b) = 1,
i.e., the (a,b)-benzel admits exactly one such tiling (and in this tiling every tile is a right-pointing stone).
artifact.status_search_result: The conjecture has been resolved affirmatively. Follow-up work on benzel tilings (notably the "Tilings of benzels via the abacus bijection" paper and related works on generalized compression) establishes that when a+b ≡ 1 (mod 3), the Conway–Lagarias invariant equals the area of the region, forcing every tile to be a right-pointing stone, hence T_{1,1,3}(a,b) = 1.

status_evidence.title: Tilings of Benzels via the Abacus Bijection
status_evidence.snippet: Resolves several of Propp's benzel tiling conjectures, including uniqueness results in the residue class a+b ≡ 1 (mod 3).
status_evidence.claim: The uniqueness conjecture for T_{1,1,3}(a,b) when a+b ≡ 1 mod 3 is proved.

status_evidence.title: Tilings of Benzels via Generalized Compression
status_evidence.snippet: Further establishes tiling enumeration results for benzels, including cases where only right stones are forced.
status_evidence.claim: Confirms the unique-tiling case in the relevant residue class.
